Carol Brod

Carol Brod

Carol Brod  

A biographical analysis of a major historical figure necessarily focuses on central themes and leans on major events to build an understanding of the direction, the meaning, the enduring impact of the life. In the wake of his definitive Freud: A Life for Our Time, Peter Gay has presented us with some additional anecdotes and deeper looks at some more peripheral areas of Freud's existence. These outtakes from Gay's earlier work further illuminate Freud, the man.

Freud: Explorations and Entertainments, Gay's “final farewell” to Freud, takes us on excursions through the intricate byways of Freud's mind. We are provided with maps which help us to travel from the small paths of passions to the royal road which leads to the discovery of Sigmund Freud, the whole man. Our enjoyable tour of some of Freud's interests and his pleasures adds to our understanding of the man and his thought.

Our journey begins with the question of who wrote Shakespeare's plays. While many cultured Viennese of the day had some interest in this popular issue, Gay describes Freud's obsession with the identification of Shakespeare as the Earl of Oxford as “one of the two most eccentric commitments of his life,” the other being the identification of Moses as an Egyptian. He speculates that as he grew older, Freud suffered the “torment of the incomplete,” as his hope failed that the accumulation of his theoretical ideas would bind into a coherent whole.

In this book Giovacchini shows us how he works with difficult patients ranging on a developmental continuum from inchoate states to higher level character disorders. He tells us what happened in the sessions, what his countertransference feelings were, what motivated his interventions, and what the outcome was. Using mostly his own work, but also occasionally contributions from colleagues or supervisees, he demonstrates how the careful study and the proper management of countertransference feelings will bring about therapeutic results however disruptive the patients may be. He is not afraid to let us see occasionally a temporary misjudgment: what appears at first to be a catastrophe may turn into a triumph. The abundant, well-documented and engrossing clinical illustrations are framed by the author's theoretical concepts; technique and countertransference are inseparable.

Giovacchini's therapeutic model is based on Winnicott's: he emphasizes the roles of a soothing holding environment and nurturing interpretations. Informed by the countertransference feelings, these interpretations either of the defenses or of the motivations behind them are maturational interventions, felt as “a good feed” by the patient.

Giovacchini divides countertransference into two broad categories. He calls the first “homogeneous countertransference reactions” and the second “idiosyncratic responses.” (These roughly correspond to objective and subjective countertransference.) Both kinds fluctuate and may be mixed at various times in various degrees. Either can be disruptive or nondisruptive and, in some instances, idiosyncratic responses may be a valuable asset. In general, the more primitive the psychic organization of a patient, the more intense the countertransference will be; however, intense countertransference responses do not hinder treatment or render it impossible.

This psychobiography of the renowned English poet, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, reads as if it were a novel as it chronicles the events in the life of the man who, along with his contemporary, William Wordsworth, fathered modern poetry and the romantic revolution in literature. Weissman traces the life of the famous poet from earliest childhood to the end of his life, covering the familiar facts of Coleridge's addiction to opium, his failed love of Sara Hutchinson, and his close relationship with William Wordsworth, the other dominant influence on English literature at the time.

Weissman's special contribution to an understanding of Coleridge is his focus on the personal, unconscious myth that is repeated throughout Coleridge's life. This myth is the story of Cain and Abel, symbolically dramatized in the crowning achievement of Coleridge's career, the epic poem “The Rhyme of the Ancient Mariner.” According to Weissman, the myth became a significant factor in Coleridge's life when he was seven: blinded by rage, he seized a kitchen knife and lunged at his tormenting older brother. Aroused by the commotion, his mother arrived just in time to catch her son's arm and pry the knife from his fist. Caught in the act, and aware that nothing he might say to his mother could justify the attack, he wrestled free from her grip and bolted from the house into the stormy autumn evening. The boy was found and brought home to his joyous parents. So happy to have him safe, no one mentioned the fight or the knife. With careful nursing, the child recovered from the physical exposure and shock within a few days. But thoughts of his encounter with his brother and his ordeal remained buried inside of him. And although he received no further punishment for his deed, memories would echo and re-echo within him for the rest of his life. Having struck out murderously against his brother, he would for the rest of his life feel the mark of Cain.

Coleridge began to learn to curb and disguise his unbridled aggressive instincts. Eventually, he would go overboard in his attempts to control his arrogance and suppress his competitiveness. He would make it a point of honor to deny his own self-interest, even to the extent of refusing to stand up for himself and fight back when it was appropriate to do so.

I imagine that any publisher would salivate at the prospect of producing a book with this title. The private letters of James Strachey and his wife, Alix, written during the period when she was residing in Berlin, the Capital of Decadence, undergoing psychoanalysis with Karl Abraham, and he was in London just starting his own psychoanalytic practice and his translations of Freud, exchanging the news and gossip of both the psychoanalytic community and the Bloomsbury world—how delicious!

The reader, too, upon first viewing the book, experiences the thrill of anticipation. This book promises the sexual and moral decadence of Bloomsbury, celebrated in the ambiguous works of Virginia Woolf, the oeuvres of the Sitwells, and the novels of E. M. Forster, illuminated by the light of psychoanalysis. What a feast!

Introduction

In her eighth session, Ms. A reported a dream for the first time: “I way lying down and a bird was sitting on my shoulder interrupting me.” I understood this as a clear communication regarding my activity in the sessions.

This dream focused my attention on the question of when I should talk or be quiet, which I knew could have some subjective elements. In my family, where everyone was always talking, it had been difficult for me to get a word in and I had developed a hesitancy about when to talk. If I talked when they stopped, the timing was often off because their pauses usually occurred at moments of tension. Now I sensed that this problem could interfere with my functioning as an effective analyst.

When I began seeing patients, it was hard not to talk every five minutes; I felt I had to demonstrate my analytic knowledge. Supervision helped me to listen to the patient, to understand that my role was to listen in such a way that the patient could say everything. Yet I knew there was a difference of opinion among analysts as to how to do this.

The discussion of timing in the psychoanalytic literature deals mainly with the readiness of patients to receive an interpretation, not with their need for contact from the analyst. However, there are indications of wide concern about the dilemma of talking versus free-floating attention (Fenichel, 1941), and there is general agreement that the analyst needs to use tact, empathy, and clinical judgment as a basis for knowing when to intervene.

This book presents a clinical and theoretical description of the etiology and treatment of the borderline and narcissistic disorders, based on the ideas of the British and object relations schools of thought. It provides a clear, concise rendering of the application of object relations theory to the treatment of patients and the supervision of therapists. It offers the student of modern psychoanalysis a good basis for comparison of the theories and techniques of both schools of thought, which have many areas of agreement.

Three general assumptions underlie Rinsley's discussion of the borderline and narcissistic personality disorders: these types of personality disorders arise from preoedipal developmental arrest; the narcissistic personality is a more advanced or better organized version of the borderline personality; and these personality disorders arise as a result of significant impairment of the separation-individuation process. This process begins at about six months and relates to the growing child's understanding of himself as a being different from other entities.

Rinsley bases his discussion on what he calls a “mixed model” approach that utilizes “classical metapsychological principles while incorporating newer path-blazing concepts derived from the original and creative contributions of the British school.

In this book the author addresses a timely and important task—the synthesis of the recent findings of infant research with psychoanalytic theory. He begins with the statement “Psychoanalytic theory at its core is a theory of structured motivation, not a theory of structure.” This, upon reflection, is a point well made. Historically, the main thing that has attracted the interest of clinicians and the public at large in psychoanalysis is the notion that psychoanalysis explains why people do what they do.

Lichtenberg reminds us that the psychoanalytic theory of motivation had its origins with Freud's theory of instinctual drives. But at this point in time, almost a hundred years after Freud's major contribution, our theory of motivation, the author observes, is in acute disarray. Over the years psychoanalysts have felt compelled to postulate sources of motivation that compete with or even replace Eros and Thanatos. Even Freud recognized the traumatic experience (in which the ego learns to react with anxiety to similar experiences in the future) as a source of motivation.

The possibility of other sources of motivation, such as “autonomous ego functions,” “the organizing potential of object relations,” or “the dominant mass of ideas,” has encouraged fragmentation of the field into rival schools of thought identified chiefly by the source (or sources) of motivation their adherents view as central to their understanding of human dynamics. Thus we have drive-theory analysts vs. object relations analysts, existential analysts vs. Freudian analysts, classical analysts vs. modern analysts, and so on.

Introduction

During the eight years of treatment presented in this paper, specific transference/countertransference constellations were identified within which feelings induced in the analyst were used as effective therapeutic tools to resolve the patient's resistance to analytic progress. The most crucial and lengthy of these periods involved the positive and negative narcissistic transference/countertransference. The management of this very difficult phase illustrates the theory that the development, intensification, and working through of the narcissistic transference/countertransference phase is critical for the development of the capacity for object-relatedness. Introduction

All psychoanalysts sooner or later must deal with patients whose intense, unacknowledged suicidal and homicidal wishes lead them to commit self-destructive or object-destructive acts.

The transference resistance of such patients inevitably generates murderous or suicidal countertransference feelings.

My resistances to feeling suicidal and homicidal feelings were reflected in my treatment of Mrs. A. These resistances were progresively resolved in supervision and in my own treatment.

Mrs. A generated powerful negative feelings. Both her ex-husband and her daughter attempted suicide.

My original attempts to deal with her negative feelings were unsuccessful. I was either obliterating them at the source (by comforting her or trying to “fix” her) or not experiencing them (by falling asleep).

Working with Mrs. A. was especially challenging for me because of my perception that she and my mother shared significant personality traits and dynamics. My conscious and unconscious wishes to get rid of the patient may have been mitigated by my sense that treating her was helping me in an unresolved conflict with my mother. I was gradually able to separate from the original and the countertransference object by allowing myself to feel rage at both.

Nursery school teachers ask about the whole range of psychoanalytic issues. Even three- and four-year-olds wonder about the big questions in life: Why do I have to go to school? Why can't I play now? Why is my mother leaving me here? Does the teacher like me?

In the spirit of Anna Freud, who worked with young children and learned from them the true meaning of her father's theories, Erna Furman takes us into the classroom setting of nursery-age children. Her vast experience both with Anna Freud in London and at the Hannah Perkins Therapeutic Nursery School in Cleveland, helps us to understand the basic struggles involved in adjusting to nursery school. The roots of instructional conflicts are seen in the preschooler's struggles to develop a healthy ego and the need to feel whole. How children in this age group cope with anger, fear, depression, loss of love, and abandonment tells us a great deal about their need for understanding and support.

Erna Furman's basic approach is to help the three- and four-year-olds to put their feelings into words. The role of the teacher is to help the youngster find his place in the nursery school setting by clearly explaining school procedures, obligations, and responsibilities. Three- and four-year-olds are encouraged to say what they feel in a safe environment that encourages the healthy exchange of positive and negative feelings.

Each chapter deals with a specific topic and is written by a mental health practitioner who specializes in that area. They can be read as a narrative of early childhood development or used as a reference on specific issues arising in the preschool stage of development. Approached in the framework of psychoanalytic insights into early childhood behavior, the authors deal with a wide range of topics. They include the basic roles of parents and teachers, discipline, preparation for kindergarten, sex differences, characteristics of toddlers' speech, the exceptional child, and special nursery school settings.

The experience of hopelessness when treating the aging woman may reside more in the therapist than in the patient. In other words, when the therapist believes the patients is not treatable this idea may not be a comment on the patient but on the reactions of the therapist. This hypothetical orientation shapes my work with patients and is especially applicable to therapy with the aging patient, where issues of hopelessness frequently pervade the therapeutic relationship. A 63-year-old woman, Mrs. Z. came into therapy several years previous to the period of this study. She began treatment to deal with her inability to cope with her husbands's infidelity. I once made the acquaintance of a young woman whom I was very eager to impress. So I tried to think of what I had that I could impress her with.

In December of 1928, Freud, a man of seventy-two, received a letter from Ida Fliess shortly after the death of her husband:1

You perhaps have in your possession letters from Wilhelm addressed to you before your relations became clouded. They probably were not destroyed, although they have lost their meaning for you. If that is the case, would you be good enough and trusting enough, dear professor, to place them in my hands? For I am the person who of all people has the deepest interest in them. Freud responded:

I hasten to answer your letter, although I cannot at present communicate anything decisive with regard to fulfilling your request. I beg you, therefore, to allow me time over Christmas. Whatever I find will be at your disposal, unconditionally.

The school of thought known as modern psychoanalysis has established a distinct body of theory and technique, which has produced a flowering of new attitudes and applications within psychoanalysis, especially in relation to the narcissistic patient. And it appears to have still more original ideas germinating and about to burst to life—for example, the ideas of Spotnitz and many of his colleagues on the anaclitic countertransference, which may well prove to be an entirely new way of thinking about one part of the transference/countertransference matrix.

At this point it may be worthwhile to look about us at the ground we stand on, and to consider the fertile soild into which these new seeds are to be sown.

The central achievement of the modern psychoanalytic work by Spotnitz and others, the application of psychoanalytic therapy to the narcissistic disorders, was built on original, pioneering work in the area of emotional induction and emotional communication, from patient to analyst and analyst to patient. Spotnitz's first public remarks on the usefulness of induced emotions in resistance analysis were made in a talk he gave in 1949 (Spotnitz, 1976). When a patient recently asked “Why did I have so much trouble learning math in school?,” “Negligent teachers!” was the thought that instantly flew into my mind. When this patient was a student, he, like countless others, brought formidable resistances to any educator attempting to work with him. Yet isn't it the teacher's responsibility

114

to find some way to enable learning to occur? Learning and Education: Psychoanalytic Perspectives corroborates the view that an understanding of how to work with the unconscious processes of transference and resistance is essential to effective teaching: “In the last analysis any educational program rests on the faculty's ability to perceive correctly and to differentiate the ever-changing objective and subjective elements in the teaching situation” (p. 945). The thirty-two articles in this book richly review and examine the psy-chodynamics of education—learning, teaching, and knowing. Most important, the book adds to the slim but growing body of literature documenting the emotional needs of students and the psychody-namic processes in every learning situation, as well as the rationale for psychoanalytic training for teachers.

There is much to be valued in this book for psychoanalysts as well as teachers, for we are all educators concerned with helping our analysands and students develop the courage to feel ignorant—the “courage to try” (p. 143). Wolf, a self psychologist, finding that the sequence “emergence-disruption-restoration” functions in the educational situation just as in the analytic one, emphasizes the Kohutian view that a mirroring self-object gives students the “psychological oxygen” necessary to learn. Schwartz sees preoedipal influences as determining overall psychological structure, and hence the person's view of himself as “capable of learning, or, in pathological circumstances, as one who should not, ought not, or cannot learn” (p. 513). This is an interesting book filled with a wealth of theoretical concepts and clinical observations. Dr. Lewes comprehensively reviews the psychoanalytic literature on homosexuality: he both presents the

277

scope of psychoanalytic thinking on the subject and gives the reader a sense of the dynamics underlying the formation of the theory. He traces theoretical developments from Freud and his circle to current times. His work provides an informative overview of a subject that is still not fully grasped.

Dr. Lewes divides his overview into four sections. The first, beginning with Freud and extending into the 1930s, presents the oedipal theory of homosexuality. This era is overlapped by the “oral period,” which was inaugurated by the work of Melanie Klein and added to by the theories of Glover and Bergler. During this stage, homosexuality was viewed as an expression of preoedipal dynamics. This is followed by a “conservative period,” marked by the publication of the Kinsey Report and extending into the 1960s to the publication of the Bieber study: the focus is on environmental factors, which represents a shift in emphasis to the examination of interpersonal relations and social interaction. The fourth and final section encapsulates developments from the 1970s into the 1980s under the headings “The Turnaround” and “New Beginnings.” The integration of theories highlighting both oedipal and preoedipal factors as well as the roles of the aggressive and libidinal drives are discussed, as is the influence of social forces on psychoanalytic thinking.

The growth and development of the psychoanalytic theory of male homosexuality is reflective of the growth and development in psychoanalysis in general from classical to modern thinking, and illustrates the ongoing struggle that analysts have engaged in to rise above personal and cultural resistances to achieve objective understanding.

It is interesting to note that the term homosexuality did not come into popular usage until the twentieth century. The initial task for Freud and his circle was to define what exactly was signified by this term. Freud had a primary interest in understanding human sexual development, and to him homosexuality simply represented one natural outcome of the oedipus complex. He did not consider homosexuality to be a perversion, nor did he consider homosexuals to be sick. He did not equate homosexuality and pathology, and he opposed separating out homosexuals as a group or clinical entity. He strongly opposed barring them from psychoanalytic training; to him homosexuality represented an inhibition in sexual development alone. Freud believed that understanding the homosexual outcome of the oedipus complex was as important as understanding the heterosexual outcome. He stated that the task of changing either outcome to the other by psychoanalysis would be of equal difficulty.

Introduction

The concept of the therapeutic alliance has existed in the shadow of transference through most of the history of psychoanalysis but, as has been the case with its relative, countertransference, it is now beginning to emerge from the shadows to become enfranchised as a powerful and significant element in treatment. The early analysts, including Freud himself, were aware of the subtle dialectic between the need for an ascetic rigor in the analytic setting, on one hand, and the need for humanism on the other. This latter element, the need for analytic humanism, gradually evolved into the therapeutic alliance—working alliance—real relationship concepts, and finally one aspect branched off to reunite with analytic technique in the form of the empathic approach of Self-Psychology. Needless to say, the issue of parameters always lurked over the shoulder of analytic humanism creating perpetual grounds for suspicion of any technical deviations or aberrations which would contaminate the purity of the ascetic approach.

No presentation of classical psychoanalytic technique ever mentions that it is drastically different from Freud's technique. On the contrary, at least implicity one is left with the impression that one is facing a technique which had been determined exactly that way by Freud himself. And would you not expect Freud to be the classical psychoanalyst par excellence?

Only in the last few years do we read criticism by classical analysts of the technique which Freud used, as it can be gathered from his own case histories and from reports by former patients. The criticism mentions “unanalytic” interventions and suggestive steps, many of which Freud described with his characteristic frankness. The Ratman case, for example, has been mentioned by critics because of Freud's frequent deviations from the prescribed passive attitude of the analyst. He occasionally provided food for the patient, gave him a book to read, gave him moral support and reassured him about the unblemished record of the Freud family when the patient expressed doubts about it.

These differences from classical technique are now designated in the literature as technical mistakes, which can be excused by the fact that Freud was the first analyst and, for lack of experience, was bound to make mistakes. Because of these unanalytic interventions, some critics feel the Ratman case is not an example of psychoanalysis, but a case of psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy. The differences between Freud's and today's classical techniques (“psychoanalysis as we understand it today,” in the words of Charles Brenner) supposedly indicate the progress of analytic skill since Freud. The students left the teacher behind.

I was already seated on the bus when I saw Mrs. G boarding. I looked at her until she recognized me and then we said hello. With a little nervous laugh the patient sat near me. Then there was an interminable silence for about four blocks that seemed like hours. I looked toward the front of the bus, waiting to ring the bell for my bus stop. Mrs. G looked out the side window. As I left I said I would see her on Tuesday (her regular appointment day).

I felt extremely inadequate that, after two and a half years of treating this patient, I had not known how to put us both at ease and enable us to have a superficial conversation. I worried that the patient would think I was overeating. I was mildly uneasy that the patient had seen the exact neighborhood in which I lived. I was only glad that the patient had not seen the shopping bag from the unprestigious clothes store which had been obscured by the ice cream bag I was also carrying.

I felt sure that the patient would go home and gossip with her husband (whom I see with the patient in marital sessions) about how terrible I had looked. I also had a strong fear that the patient would no longer want me as her analyst now that she had seen me this way.

How much of this was objective and how much subjective narcissistic countertransference, and did one feed the other?

I had been feeling overweight, tired and unattractive and had finally found a dress that I could accept as looking decent on me, but not fantastic, and the store was certainly one I would never brag about. There was also some small guilt about the ice cream. I certainly had my share of self-attacking feelings.

The initial sessions with a psychoanalytic patient make evident the rationale for the particular style each analyst has of entering a relationship with a patient. For my part, when I begin an analysis, I pay attention to the simplest concerns. For example, the room should be pleasant, neither too warm nor too cool, neither too well-lit nor too dim. My style of dress is usually not extreme, nor does it attract too much of the patient's attention. I want to enter the session relaxed, that is, free enough of distractions so that I can be interested in what the patient wants to talk about. However, I don't want to be overly interested—I don't want to lean forward in my seat or hang on the person's every word. In the first session my primary interest is in why the patient is consulting me. To find out more about the problem I ask some variation on the question, “What brings you here?” It is not my intention to say much more in the early part of this session unless the patient addresses me directly with questions, or a question is necessary to make sense out of what my visitor is saying.

I find that when I act like this in the first session my visitor responds in his own style to my question “Why are you here?” He may or may not ask questions.
